item.title: PostgreSQL High Availability in 2026: Patroni, pgBouncer, and Replication Strategies
item.description: The first time a primary Postgres database went down on my watch, I had a runbook, a pager alert, and eleven minutes of downtime while I manually promoted a replica and rewired connection strings by hand. That was fine for a side project. It is not fine for anything that makes money while it’s asleep. The gap between “we have a replica” and “we have high availability” is the entire subject of this post — and it’s a bigger gap than most teams realize until the primary actually falls over at 3 AM.
